title: How precise is the estimate?
objectives: Compute and interpret a standard error.

screens.prose: Two analysts estimate the same strategy's mean daily return. Ana averages 25 days; Ben averages 400. Daily returns have sd 1%. The solid curve shows where Ben's average tends to land; the dashed one, Ana's.
screens.question: Whose average is more likely to land within 0.1% of the true mean?

options.why: You favoured the short record. Ana's curve is four times wider, so her average strays further.

options.text: Equally likely: both aim at the same mean
options.why: Both curves centre on the truth, but Ana's is far wider. Aiming right is not the same as landing close.

hints.text: Which curve is packed more tightly round the true mean?
The solid curve is Ben's; the dashed one is Ana's.
Ben's curve is the narrow one. More of it lies within 0.1% of the centre.

feedback.correct: Ben's average lands within 0.1% about 95% of the time; Ana's only about 38%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how tightly each curve hugs the centre.

explain.text: Both curves centre on the truth, 0.05%. Ben's is four times narrower, so it lands within 0.1% about 95% of the time, against 38% for Ana. Quantity of data buys precision.

screens.prose: A strategy truly earns 0.05% a day, with daily sd 1%. The curve is the distribution of its average return over $n$ days. The shaded band is within 0.1% of the truth. Slide $n$ and watch the spread.
screens.question: The spread is 0.2% at $n = 25$. What is it at $n = 100$, in %?

widget.accept: 0.1: four times the days halves the spread
widget.label: Spread at 100 days, in percent

hints.text: Slide to 100 and read the caption.
The caption prints the spread for the current $n$.
At $n = 100$ the caption reads 0.100%.

feedback.correct: Four times the data, half the spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $n$ to 100 and read the spread in the caption.

byKey.linear: You divided by 4 because $n$ grew fourfold. The caption shows the spread only halves.
byKey.same: That is the spread at 25 days. Slide $n$ up to 100.
byKey.sd: 1% is the sd of a single day. The average is much less spread out.

explain.text: At $n = 100$ the spread is 0.1%, half its value at 25 days. Quadrupling $n$ halved it, so the spread falls like $1/\sqrt n$. To halve it again you need 400 days.

screens.prose: That spread is the **standard error** of the mean: $\mathrm{SE}(\bar x) = \sigma/\sqrt n$. It says how far an estimate typically lands from the truth. Another strategy has daily sd $\sigma = 1.5\%$, shown as one day's curve, and a 36-day record.
screens.question: What is the standard error of its mean daily return, in %?

hints.text: Divide the daily sd by something that grows with the record.
The curve is one day. The average of 36 days is narrower.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\sigma$ by $\sqrt n$.

byKey.by-n: You divided by $n = 36$. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{36} = 6$.
byKey.sd: 1.5% is the spread of a single day. The average of 36 days varies less.
byKey.var: You divided the variance, $1.5^2 = 2.25$, by 36. That is $\mathrm{SE}^2$; take its square root.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = 1.5/\sqrt{36} = 0.25\%$. The dashed curve is the average of 36 days: six times narrower than one day. It is the same curve you slid on the last screen.

screens.prose: In practice $\sigma$ is unknown. We plug in the sample sd $s$, so the estimated standard error is $s/\sqrt n$. A 49-day backtest reports these figures.
screens.question: What is the estimated standard error of the mean, in %?

hints.text: Which row plays the part of $\sigma$?
The sample sd stands in for $\sigma$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $s$ by $\sqrt n$.

byKey.sd: 1.4% is the spread of single days. The mean of 49 days is seven times steadier.
byKey.mean: You divided the mean by 7. The standard error comes from the spread $s$, not from $\bar x$.

explain.text: $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}} = 1.4/\sqrt{49} = 0.2\%$. The mean, 0.08%, is less than half a standard error from zero. This backtest cannot yet tell its edge from noise.

screens.prose: A strategy has traded for one day and returned 0.7%. Its sample sd is $s = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2/(n - 1)}$.
screens.question: What is the estimated standard error of the mean?

options.text: There is none: $s$ needs at least two days

options.why: You used the one return as its own spread. A single number shows where it is, not how much it varies.

options.text: 0%, since one day shows no spread
options.why: One day shows no spread, but that is not certainty. The formula gives $0/0$, which is undefined.

hints.text: Work out $n - 1$ for one day.
The sd row is what the standard error needs.
With $n = 1$ the sum is 0 and $n - 1 = 0$, so $s = \sqrt{0/0}$ is undefined.

feedback.correct: One observation gives no estimate of spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try computing $s$ with $n = 1$.

explain.text: With one day, $\bar x = 0.7$, the only deviation is 0 and $n - 1 = 0$. So $s = \sqrt{0/0}$, undefined, and so is $s/\sqrt n$. You need at least two observations to measure uncertainty from the data.

screens.prose: A hit rate is a mean too: each day scores 1 if a signal was right, 0 if not. One day then has variance $p(1 - p)$, so $\mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$.
screens.question: What is the standard error of the hit rate?

widget.label: Standard error of the hit rate

hints.text: Find $\hat p(1 - \hat p)$ first.
$0.24/150 = 0.0016$, and its square root is 0.04.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n$, then take the square root.

byKey.no-root: That is $\mathrm{SE}^2$. Take its square root.
byKey.sd: $\sqrt{0.24} = 0.49$ is the spread of one day's 0 or 1. Divide by $n$ inside the root.
byKey.p-over-n: You divided $\hat p$ by $n$. The variance of one day is $\hat p(1 - \hat p)$.

explain.text: $\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4/150} = \sqrt{0.0016} = 0.04$. So 60% is uncertain by about 4 percentage points. That is the same $s/\sqrt n$ rule, with $s^2 = \hat p(1 - \hat p)$.

screens.prose: A strategy's 100 daily returns have sample sd 2%. A colleague says: our estimate of the mean daily return could easily be 2% out. The curve shows the spread of single days.
screens.question: How far off is the estimated mean, typically?

options.why: You used the spread of single days. The mean of 100 days varies ten times less: $2\%/\sqrt{100}$.
You divided by $n = 100$. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
You divided the variance, 4, by 100. Take the square root of that: 0.2%.

hints.text: Is 2% the spread of a day or of an average?
The curve is single days, not the mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The question is about the mean of 100 days, not about one day.

byKey.sd: You confused the standard deviation with the standard error. The sd describes single days; the SE describes the mean of 100 of them.

explain.text: The sd, 2%, is how much single days vary. The standard error, $2/\sqrt{100} = 0.2\%$, is how much the 100-day mean varies. The dashed curve is that mean: ten times narrower.

screens.prose: Each time you divided a spread by $\sqrt n$: $$\mathrm{SE}(\bar x) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt n}, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}{n}}.$$ A volatility estimate has $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\sigma) \approx \hat\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$; we state that one without proof.
screens.question: Your SE is 0.2% from 100 days. How many days in all would give an SE of 0.1%?

options.why: You expected the SE to fall in line with $n$. Doubling $n$ cuts it only by $\sqrt 2$, to 0.14%.
You scaled $n$ by $\sqrt 2$. Halving $1/\sqrt n$ needs $\sqrt n$ to double, so $n$ quadruples.

hints.text: How did the spread change on the slider when $n$ went from 25 to 100?
Halving the SE needs $\sqrt n$ to double.
$\sqrt n$ doubles when $n$ quadruples: $4 \times 100$.

feedback.correct: Four times the days halves the SE.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The SE scales like $1/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} \propto 1/\sqrt n$, so halving it needs $\sqrt n$ to double. That means $4 \times 100 = 400$ days. Each extra digit of precision costs a hundred times the data.

screens.prose: Show where $\sigma/\sqrt n$ comes from. Days $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are independent, each with variance $\sigma^2$, and $\bar X = \tfrac1n \sum X_i$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \mathrm{Var}\left(\tfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)$, the definition of $\bar X$
$= \tfrac{1}{n^2}\,\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)$, a constant leaves a variance squared
$\mathrm{SE}(\bar X) = \sigma/\sqrt n$, the square root of the variance

hints.text: Start from the definition of $\bar X$.
Pull the $\tfrac1n$ out before you split the sum.
Constant out (squared), split by independence, count $n$ copies of $\sigma^2$, take the root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the constant out first, then use independence.

explain.text: The $\tfrac1n$ comes out squared, independence splits the sum, and $n$ copies of $\sigma^2$ leave $\sigma^2/n$. The square root gives $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Independence is doing real work: correlated days would not add like this.

screens.prose: A strategy's backtest covers 250 trading days. Its daily returns have sd 1%, and its mean daily return is 0.05%.
screens.question: What is the standard error of its mean daily return, in %?

hints.text: Which two rows does the standard error use?
Days and the daily sd.
$\sqrt{250} \approx 15.81$, so $\mathrm{SE} = 1/15.81$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the daily sd by $\sqrt{250}$.

byKey.by-n: You divided by 250. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{250} \approx 15.8$.
byKey.sd: 1% is one day's spread. A year's average is much steadier.
byKey.ratio: That is the mean in standard errors, $0.05/0.063$. The question asks for the SE itself.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = 1/\sqrt{250} = 0.063\%$. The mean, 0.05%, is only 0.79 standard errors above zero. A whole year of data cannot tell this edge from luck.

screens.prose: A trader won 55 of 100 trades. If their true hit rate were 50%, the curve shows where a 100-trade hit rate would land.
screens.question: Using $\hat p = 0.55$, how many standard errors above 50% is the hit rate?

hints.text: Find the SE of $\hat p$ first.
The curve's spread is about one SE.
$\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{0.2475/100} = 0.0497$; divide the gap 0.05 by it.

feedback.correct: About one standard error: barely distinguishable from a coin flip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gap, $0.55 - 0.5$, by $\sqrt{0.55 \times 0.45/100}$.

byKey.sd: You divided by $\sqrt{0.2475} = 0.497$, the spread of one trade. Divide by $n$ inside the root.
byKey.points: 5 is the gap in percentage points. Express it in standard errors.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{0.55 \times 0.45/100} = 0.0497$, so 55% is about 1.0 SE above 50%. A coin-flipper beats 55% about 16% of the time, the shaded tail. Polls work the same way: 1,000 voters give a margin of about 3 points.

ideas: The standard error is the spread of an estimate's sampling distribution: how far it typically lands from the truth.
For a mean, $\mathrm{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt n$, estimated by $s/\sqrt n$; for a proportion, $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$.
The SE falls like $1/\sqrt n$: four times the data halves it.

formula.name: Standard error of a mean
formula.note: For a volatility estimate, $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\sigma) \approx \hat\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$. One observation gives no estimate.

summary.trap: The sd describes single observations; the SE describes the estimate. And doubling $n$ cuts the SE only by $\sqrt 2$.

quiz.prose: A poll of 1,000 voters finds 52% support for a candidate.
quiz.question: What is the standard error of that 52%?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$.

byKey.no-root: That is the variance of $\hat p$. Take its square root.
byKey.sd: That is the spread of one voter's yes or no. Divide by $n$ inside the root.

explain.text: $\sqrt{0.52 \times 0.48/1000} = 0.0158$. Two standard errors is about 3 points, the margin of error polls quote. So 52% cannot be told apart from 50% with confidence.

quiz.prose: A desk estimates a stock's daily volatility as $\hat\sigma = 1.5\%$ from 450 daily returns.
quiz.question: About what is the standard error of that estimate?

options.why: You used $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$. A volatility estimate has $\sqrt{2n}$ underneath.
You divided by $n$. The standard error divides by a square root.
That is the volatility itself, not the uncertainty in estimating it.

explain.text: $2n = 900$ and $\sqrt{900} = 30$, so $\mathrm{SE} \approx 1.5/30 = 0.05\%$. The volatility is pinned to within a few percent of itself, far better than a mean.

quiz.prose: From 50 days, a mean daily return has standard error 0.3%.
quiz.question: What is the standard error from 200 days, with a similar sd?

options.why: You divided by 4 because $n$ grew fourfold. The SE falls with $\sqrt n$, so it halves.
The SE depends on $n$. More days give a steadier mean.
That divides by $\sqrt 2$. Here $n$ quadrupled, so divide by $\sqrt 4 = 2$.

feedback.correct: Four times the days, half the SE.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The SE scales like $1/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: $200/50 = 4$ and $\sqrt 4 = 2$, so the SE halves from 0.3% to 0.15%.

quiz.prose: You keep adding days to a backtest and recompute the sample sd $s$ and the standard error $s/\sqrt n$ each time.
quiz.question: What happens as $n$ grows?

options.text: $s$ settles near $\sigma$; the standard error shrinks towards 0

options.why: You treated $s$ as an uncertainty. It estimates the daily spread $\sigma$, which more data does not reduce.
The standard error has $\sqrt n$ underneath, so it keeps falling.
That swaps the two. Days stay as noisy as ever; only the average steadies.

feedback.correct: The data stay noisy; the average steadies.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which one has $\sqrt n$ in its formula.

explain.text: $s$ estimates how much single days vary, and that does not change with more days. The standard error $s/\sqrt n$ falls towards 0. Confusing the two is the commonest error in reading a backtest.
